transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Aisha (Redwood CSM); Priya, Daniel, Marta, Oliver (Saffron)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):
- Customer requirements: private VPC deployment with EU data residency, SOC 2 / ISO audit evidence, SSO with OIDC/SAML, strict RBAC, 3-year audit log retention for certain records, bring-your-own-KMS (HSM optional).
- Key risks discussed: egress control, lateral movement prevention, KMS key rotation & key provenance, per-request PII scrubbing and telemetry, SIEM integration for audit logs.
- Agreed next steps: send SOC artifacts, provide network ACL examples, schedule pilot and perf baseline.

Topics:
- Private control plane vs fully air-gapped
- Network isolation patterns: egress proxies, private endpoints, no public outbound
- KMS integration: AWS KMS vs customer HSM and key-handshake flows
- SSO / RBAC: SAML assertions and role mapping
- Audit logging and retention: syslog, Splunk/Datadog sinks, per-token provenance

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll try to cover the architecture and compliance asks, and, um, leave time for Qs.
[00:18] Priya Nair: hi thanks, yeah we put this together because Saffron is evaluating private runtime options. main things: SOC 2 readiness obviously, iso 27k requirements, and most importantly we need complete control over egress.
[00:33] Marcus Chen: great, can you give a quick summary of your existing stack and where you'd run the customer-managed bits? e.g., is this in an AWS VPC, on-prem, hybrid?
[00:42] Oliver Beckett: we're primarily in AWS eu-west-1, we run core infra in a set of private subnets behind transit gateway. we do have a colo footprint for a handful of workloads but this will live in the VPC.
[00:55] Marta Kowalski: for compliance, any logs touching personal data need three years retention and immutability for a subset, and we need chain-of-custody for keys — so bring-your-own-kms with HSM-backed keys is preferred.
[01:12] Marcus Chen: ok that matches what others have asked. our Private control plane can be run as a customer-managed control plane inside your VPC or we can offer a private-hosted control plane that talks over a single egress channel; both options support BYOK patterns.
[01:28] Daniel Ruiz: pause — by "control plane" you mean the Redwood management/control UI or something else? can you clarify what traffic needs to leave our network?
[01:36] Lena Ortiz: good question — short version: the customer-managed control plane keeps all decisioning inside your network; the Redwood control plane is optional. if you run the private/control-plane inside your VPC, runtime nodes never initiate outbound to public internet except for KMS endpoints if you choose cloud KMS. if you want truly air-gapped, we can support an on-prem package with no outbound egress.
[01:58] Priya Nair: so we want minimal outbound. our security team requires egress to only approved destinations via an egress proxy that does TLS inspection and logging.
[02:08] Marcus Chen: yep that's common. recommended pattern: deploy an egress proxy (squid/charon type or managed egress gateway) in an isolated subnet, force NAT through that proxy, and whitelist only the necessary endpoints — e.g., your KMS VPC endpoints, internal telemetry collectors, and Redwoods-compatible update endpoints if you opt in. note — redwood's product sometimes shows up in docs as "Redwood Private" or "Redwood control plane" which autofills weirdly in transcripts.
[02:35] Oliver Beckett: scratch — we will not allow any public ip for runtime nodes, so the proxy will be the only path. can we do VPC endpoints for S3-like model artifact stores?
[02:44] Marcus Chen: yes VPC endpoints and S3 gateway endpoints are supported; model artifacts can be pulled via interface endpoints. for large model pulls we also support S3 presigned URLs tunneled over the private az endpoints.
[02:56] Priya Nair: about KMS: we use a CloudHSM cluster today and require HSM-backed key usage for any production crypto ops. how does Redwood integrate with that?
[03:06] Marcus Chen: two integrations: 1) if you have AWS KMS backed by CloudHSM and allow KMS API, we can call the KMS API from the runtime nodes restricted to your account and key arn. 2) for stricter setups, we support a key-unwrap flow where the customer signs a CSR and we perform local crypto operations with keys never leaving HSM — basically a BYOK hybrid handshake. note there are performance implications for per-token encryption if you do HSM every call; we typically do envelope encryption with locally cached DEKs rotated via KMS/HSM.
[03:42] Daniel Ruiz: envelope encryption sounds good, can you describe key rotation and provenance? auditors ask for rotation windows, who rotated the key, and a signed event trail.
[03:52] Marcus Chen: yes, we can write key rotation events to the audit log; the runtime emits key-rotation metadata including key id, rotation timestamp, initiating principal. if you're using cloud KMS we can ingest CloudTrail entries as well; if you're using HSM we'll provide a signed rotation certificate that can be stored in your key provenance ledger.
[04:12] Marta Kowalski: on the audit logs themselves — we need immutable logs for certain events (access to PII prompts, key unwrap, admin role changes). retention 3 years, WORM preferred. do you support writing to our Splunk / S3 WORM buckets?
[04:26] Marcus Chen: yes we support syslog, Splunk HEC, Datadog, and direct S3 writes. for WORM we'll write to an S3 bucket with object lock enabled in compliance mode, or deliver to your SIEM endpoint. note: some events are token-level and can be large; we recommend sampling for non-critical telemetry and full logging for admin/audit events.
[04:50] Priya Nair: what's the typical token-level data we log? we have to avoid logging prompt text containing PII where possible.
[04:58] Marcus Chen: good call — Redwood can redact PII at ingestion with regex/policy sets; we also support field-level redaction before logs are emitted. by default we log metadata (request id, model id, duration, node id) and only store prompts if explicitly enabled for debugging with a retention policy.
[05:18] Lena Ortiz: quick interjection, on the compliance docs, we'll send our SOC2 type II summary and an ISO gap analysis that maps to common controls in your questionnaire.
[05:26] Priya Nair: thanks, that's helpful.
[05:30] [05:30] Marta Kowalski: do you have RBAC primitives compatible with our existing SAML groups? we don't want to re-map everything.
[05:38] Marcus Chen: we support both SAML and OIDC SSO. mapping can be done via SAML attributes or OIDC groups claim. we expose role bindings: admin, operator, reader, and custom roles — you can map SAML group names to those roles. we also support attribute-based access controls for per-model restrictions.
[05:58] Daniel Ruiz: does that mean we can restrict who can call specific models or who can view model outputs? we need separation between inference operators and data reviewers.
[06:06] Marcus Chen: yes — per-route and per-model RBAC. examples: inference-service role can invoke generation APIs but not view or download full prompt logs; compliance role can view logs but surgical redaction enforced.
[06:20] Priya Nair: we have a concern: how do you prevent lateral movement if a runtime node is compromised? network-level and process-level controls?
[06:30] Marcus Chen: network: strong microsegmentation, restrict egress and inter-subnet traffic with security groups and network policies (we ship a calico policy guide), and restrict administrative ports. process: runtime runs as non-root, seccomp filters, and optional mTLS between services. also we recommend host-hardening and minimal AMI with CIS benchmarks.
[06:52] Oliver Beckett: can we get a sample network diagram with subnets, egress proxy, bastion, logging collectors — that's part of our ask for the security review.
[06:59] Lena Ortiz: we'll provide that; Marcus has a reference design that we can adapt to your VPC CIDR.
[07:06] [07:06] Marcus Chen: also note we recommend a separate management VPC for the control plane with VPC peering — control plane endpoints can be exposed via interface endpoints only. if you want more isolation we can run everything in customer VPCs with no peering and a self-managed console.
[07:23] Priya Nair: latency and cost tradeoffs? if we keep everything inside VPC and use HSM, do you see a big perf hit for inference?
[07:31] Marcus Chen: minimal for inference; the main perf surface is model weight loading and large blob transfers. HSM ops for DEK rotation add a small latency bump during rotation events, but we cache DEKs in memory and rotate asynchronously. overall inference latency will be dominated by model size and GPU utilization, not KMS calls on the hot path.
[07:52] Daniel Ruiz: about firewalling — we manage stateful firewall rules on the perimeter; do you need any inbound ports open for runtime nodes for health checks or agent heartbeats?
[08:01] Marcus Chen: runtime nodes don't require inbound from the public internet. health checks use internal control plane heartbeats over TLS. if you run the control plane outside your VPC you'd need a single egress path; otherwise no inbound.
[08:15] Priya Nair: what about model updates — how do we ensure code provenance for model artifacts? we need signed attestations and supply-chain proofs.
[08:25] Marcus Chen: we support signed model artifacts (sigstore or cosign) and we can validate signatures before loading. we also emit provenance records into audit logs for each model load including artifact hash, signature verification, and who triggered the load.
[08:42] Oliver Beckett: integration with our SIEM: we use Splunk and a logging pipeline that enforces retention tiers. can we push raw audit events to Splunk HEC over VPC endpoint?
[08:52] Marcus Chen: yes Splunk HEC over private endpoint is supported. we can also forward to Kinesis or EventBridge if you prefer native aws ingest.
[08:59] Marta Kowalski: on the SOC2 side, auditors ask for proof of least privilege and access reviews. how does Redwood support periodic attestation?
[09:09] Marcus Chen: we provide reports for role assignments, admin actions, and we can export CSVs for attestation. we also support webhook-based notifications for admin role changes.
[09:19] Priya Nair: we need to know about data residency: our PII must remain in EU and backups also. what's Redwood's current capability?
[09:27] Lena Ortiz: for Private deployments you can pin regions and ensure model runtime and artifact storage stay in selected regions; backups to S3 can be restricted to the bucket in eu-west-1 or to your on-prem backup system. we'll document the durability and retention controls.
[09:44] Daniel Ruiz: about network ACLs and firewall rules: any recommendations for egress allowlists? we want a minimal set.
[09:52] Marcus Chen: minimal egress list typically: your KMS regional endpoint, internal SIEM collector, S3 VPC endpoint, container image registry endpoints (if you pull images), and optionally a Redwood update endpoint if you accept automatic security patches. everything else should be denied.
[10:10] Priya Nair: can we do certificate pinning for control plane communications?
[10:15] Marcus Chen: yes mutual TLS with pinned CA roots is supported for control plane connections. for extra assurance we can provide key fingerprints for verification.
[10:25] [10:25] Oliver Beckett: firewall logging: do you have recommended formats and will those logs tie back to request IDs for correlation?
[10:33] Marcus Chen: we include request ids in our logs and recommend adding the same id to firewall logs via a header injected at the proxy; correlation fields we usually use: request_id, node_id, model_id, user_principal.
[10:47] Lena Ortiz: quick note — some earlier transcripts spelled our product "Redwood Private" weirdly in the automated notes; apologies for that noise.
[10:55] [10:55] Marta Kowalski: data deletion requests — if a customer asks to delete a user's data, how is that handled in the private deployment?
[11:02] Marcus Chen: when data-deletion is requested we can scrub logs and triggers based on request_id and we can rotate keys for affected datasets so that future decrypts are impossible; we support selective deletion and certifiable wipe processes, though for long-term immutable audit artifacts you might need a legal exception — we'll work through the policy.
[11:26] Priya Nair: one more on encryption: do you store any plaintext prompts on disk?
[11:30] Marcus Chen: by default prompts are in-memory only and are flushed; persistent storage is encrypted and by default we avoid storing prompt text unless you enable debug logging. if enabled, prompt archival is encrypted with your DEKs and stored only in your S3 bucket or configured store.
[11:50] [11:50] Daniel Ruiz: any recommended hardening checklist for the AMIs? we use a CIS baseline.
[11:55] Marcus Chen: we publish an AMI hardening checklist: disable unused services, enable auditd, kernel parameter hardening, seccomp and apparmor profiles — we'll include that checklist in the follow-up package.
[12:07] Priya Nair: regulatory question: if an EU regulator requests data access, do logs show geo-located handling and where data was stored?
[12:16] Marcus Chen: yes location metadata is in provenance logs; we can tag events with region and storage bucket location and include those in auditor exports.
[12:28] [12:28] Lena Ortiz: ok let's jump to a quick scenario — assume a runtime node is compromised, what detection and response steps do you want to see from us? Marcus?
[12:36] Marcus Chen: detection: we emit syscall-level alerts (if enabled), unexpected outbound connections, and auth failures; we forward to your SIEM. containment: isolate node via security group automation, revoke credentials, and rotate keys used by that node. recovery: reprovision nodes from hardened AMI and replay audit trail to verify no exfiltration.
[12:59] Marta Kowalski: can we automate key rotation on detection?
[13:03] Marcus Chen: yes we support automated rotation via a runbook trigger. it can be synchronous or quarantined for manual approve.
[13:12] [13:12] Daniel Ruiz: slightly tangential — what metrics do you collect that could help with forensic analysis?
[13:18] Marcus Chen: request traces, node process snapshots, model load events, key events, and network flows (if you enable netflow). we can keep higher-fidelity traces for a short window and lower-fidelity for long-term retention.
[13:36] Priya Nair: about SOC2 evidences, aside from configs and logs, do you provide penetration test reports or engagement summaries?
[13:44] Lena Ortiz: we provide third-party pentest summaries (high-level) and internal vuln management reports; full pentest details are shared under NDA in enterprise engagements.
[13:58] Oliver Beckett: can we get a diagram showing egress proxy placement and how the VPC endpoints are used for artifact fetch?
[14:05] Marcus Chen: yes we'll share a network diagram plus a sample iptables/acl snippet.
[14:10] [14:10] Priya Nair: one more — do you support per-tenant encryption keys for multi-tenant configs? we want strong tenant isolation.
[14:18] Marcus Chen: Private deployment supports per-tenant DEKs, each wrapped by tenant-specific KMS keys. that provides cryptographic separation; in dedicated/shared environments we offer tenant-aware isolation.
[14:33] Daniel Ruiz: timeline for pilot and what we need to supply?
[14:37] Lena Ortiz: pilot: 2 weeks of validation, we'll need a sandbox VPC with sample data (anonymized), SAML metadata, and a KMS test key. Marcus will run baseline tests.
[14:48] Priya Nair: about legal: do you sign data processing addenda and is there support for data residency clauses?
[14:56] Lena Ortiz: yes DPA and data residency clauses are standard for enterprise; legal will follow up.
[15:03] [15:03] Marta Kowalski: auditability question — we need immutable chain of custody for admin actions. do you have an admin approval workflow?
[15:12] Marcus Chen: yes we provide approval flows for critical actions; every admin action is logged with who approved it and we can produce signed attestations.
[15:25] Priya Nair: curious about costs for HSM-backed config vs cloud-kms — a ballpark?
[15:32] Marcus Chen: HSM adds some fixed costs for HSM instances plus per-operation charges; overall it's higher but often necessary for certain regulated data. we'll include a costing appendix in the follow-up.
[15:46] [15:46] Lena Ortiz: ok going into some low-level network specifics — Marcus?
[15:50] Marcus Chen: recommended CIDR layout: management VPC (10.0.0.0/24) for control plane, runtime VPC (10.0.1.0/22) with isolated subnets per AZ, egress subnet with only the proxy/nat in it, logging VPC with endpoints to SIEM. Use security groups to restrict ports and nacl for coarse-grained deny.
[16:14] Oliver Beckett: will route tables be managed by us or do you need specific routes for interface endpoints?
[16:20] Marcus Chen: customers manage their route tables; we'll provide the route proposals and interface endpoint configuration. we recommend explicit routes to interface endpoints for S3/KMS.
[16:34] Daniel Ruiz: about firewalling and iptables examples — can you share a snippet that denies all outbound and allows only endpoint ranges?
[16:42] Marcus Chen: yes example: iptables -P OUTPUT DROP; iptables -A OUTPUT -d <kms-ip> -j ACCEPT; iptables -A OUTPUT -d <siem-ip> -j ACCEPT; plus allow localhost and dhcp. we'll include examples per distro.
[16:58] Priya Nair: do you support egress FQDN allowlist (we use a lot of managed services)?
[17:05] Marcus Chen: yes via proxy — you can allow FQDNs at the proxy layer and use TLS interception with your own CA if required. for stricter, prefer IP ranges in the VPC.
[17:18] [17:18] Marta Kowalski: about compliance artifacts: will we get a mapping of Redwood controls to our internal control framework?
[17:27] Lena Ortiz: yes we'll provide a control matrix mapping Redwood product features to SOC2/ISO controls and evidence sources.
[17:36] Daniel Ruiz: any gotchas for private deployments we should know before we spin up the environment?
[17:41] Marcus Chen: watch for subnet sizing for GPU nodes (they may need ENIs and IPs), plan for ephemeral storage for cached models, ensure a robust egress proxy capacity for large model downloads, and account for VPC endpoint throughput when pulling artifacts at scale.
[18:02] Priya Nair: ok last thing — can you confirm the longest chain-of-custody retention you support via S3 WORM?
[18:10] Marcus Chen: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode supports indefinite holds; we typically recommend policy for 3+ years and archival tiers for longer.
[18:22] Lena Ortiz: we're about halfway through our time; let's surface any final high-risk items from Saffron side.
[18:30] Priya Nair: high risk is egress control and key provenance.
[18:34] Marta Kowalski: also per-request PII handling and deletion proofs.
[18:38] Marcus Chen: noted; we'll include redaction configs, proof-of-deletion patterns, and key provenance artifacts in the follow-up.
[18:46] [18:46] Oliver Beckett: I'd like to see a sample runbook for incident response that includes steps to isolate nodes and rotate keys.
[18:55] Marcus Chen: yes we'll provide that runbook and a template playbook.
[19:02] Lena Ortiz: next steps recap: Lena to share SOC2/ISO overview, Marcus to share network diagram and iptables samples, Marcus to run pilot baseline, Priya to share audit field list.
[19:16] Priya Nair: timeline ok — we'll aim to have the sandbox VPC ready by 2026-04-23.
[19:22] Lena Ortiz: perfect. any other questions?
[19:26] [19:26] Daniel Ruiz: one small question on telemetry retention costs — can you provide an estimate for 3 years at our projected throughput?
[19:34] Marcus Chen: yes Marcus will add that to the pilot deliverables.
[19:38] [19:38] Marta Kowalski: ok that's it from us.
[19:41] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot week.
[19:48] [19:48] Priya Nair: thanks. bye.
